academic.en:
## The Network Becomes the Morphology of Society

By the mid-1990s, the Internet could no longer be described solely as a new means of communication. Finance, production, governance, scientific collaboration, and cultural movements were being reorganized around electronic networks, although unevenly and within a broader transformation of capitalism. Manuel Castells attempted to describe the whole in his trilogy *The Information Age: Economy, Society and Culture*: *The Rise of the Network Society* (1996), *The Power of Identity* (1997), and *End of Millennium* (1998).

Unlike popular futurism, Castells did not declare information a new substance of history. Information and networks had existed in all societies. What was new was “informationalism”: a mode of development in which the generation, processing, and transmission of information became direct sources of productivity and power through microelectronic technologies (Castells, 1996, pp. 14–21). The network became a preferred organizational form because it combined the flexibility of decentralized units with the capacity to coordinate them in real time.

The factory of industrial society linked power to control over territory, machinery, and the discipline of working time. Network organization does not abolish those resources, but it adds the capacity to program connections: to include nodes, change routes, standardize exchange, and disconnect what is incompatible. Structure becomes dynamic. A node is significant not because of any intrinsic essence but because of its function within a particular network; the same city, firm, or person may be central in one network and peripheral in another.

## The Space of Flows

Castells contrasts the “space of places” with the space of flows: the material organization of social practices that take place simultaneously without territorial contiguity. This is not a virtuality without geography. The space of flows has at least three material layers: electronic circuits of exchange; nodes and hubs where networks connect and perform strategic functions; and the spatial organization of managerial elites able to move among those nodes (Castells, 1996, pp. 411–459).

A financial transaction passes through a cable and a computing center, is accepted within a legal jurisdiction, and affects a specific enterprise. A flow does not destroy place; it establishes an asymmetrical relationship among places. A global city becomes a node not because it is “on the Internet,” but because it concentrates infrastructure, expertise, and decision-making functions. A peripheral territory may be physically close to a cable yet socially excluded from consequential networks.

A new spatial stratification thereby emerges. Those who live and work at the tempo of global flows can switch among jurisdictions, markets, and information channels. Most people remain rooted in the space of places: housing, care, school, municipal politics, and environmental consequences cannot be transferred instantaneously. The conflict between the abstract mobility of a decision and the local irreversibility of its consequences is one of the central political tensions of the network society.

## Timeless Time

Associated with the space of flows is “timeless time,” a disruption of the sequential time of industrial modernity. Electronic markets operate continuously; messages are stored and retrieved instantaneously; a production cycle is divided across time zones; past, present, and forecast meet in an interface. This does not mean the literal disappearance of time. Rather, the network allows dominant functions to choose among acceleration, delay, repetition, and simultaneity.

Control over time is distributed unequally. Some actors obtain immediate access and the capacity to transfer risk; others wait for a decision, delivery, or authorization. Speed, like information, is a relational resource. The center's “real time” may produce prolonged uncertainty at the periphery.

## The Power of Flows and the Flows of Power

Castells's strongest formulation holds that “the power of flows takes precedence over the flows of power” (Castells, 1996, p. 469). It does not assert the disappearance of states, corporations, or classes. The point is that durable positions increasingly depend on a network logic that no single actor controls. Even a large organization must conform to financial, informational, and technological standards in order to remain included.

The impersonality of a flow does not mean that responsible actors are absent. In the conclusion to the first volume, Castells identifies the “switches” connecting networks as privileged instruments of power (Castells, 1996, pp. 470–471). Whoever establishes a standard, controls a gateway, determines compatibility, or defines a criterion of admission shapes not one message but the space of possible messages. In a later formulation, Castells distinguishes the power of those included over those excluded, the power of the network's standards, the power of actors within a network, and “network-making power”—the ability to program a network and switch its connections (Castells, 2011).

This scheme connects the preceding history. Shannon's channel establishes a physical limit on flow. TCP/IP defines the grammar of internetwork compatibility. The open Web lowers the cost of connecting a new publisher. The economics of bits concentrates value in control over access and distribution. A media environment ranks attention. Cryptography closes the contents of a flow and rearranges relations of trust. Each layer creates switching points of its own.

## Identity, Exclusion, and Counterpower

The second volume of the trilogy is necessary if society is not to be reduced to a diagram of cables. For Castells, the globalization of instrumental networks is accompanied by the intensification of identity as a source of meaning. People resist abstract flows through religious, national, territorial, gender, and environmental projects (Castells, 1997). Such movements may be defensive and exclusionary, or they may create a “project identity” capable of redefining social relations.

The network therefore does not guarantee cosmopolitanism. It can connect movements of solidarity and transnational criminal structures, scientific communities and financial speculation. Technology is “neither good, nor bad, nor neutral” in the sense that its consequences depend on a network's program, but the very possibility of programming already distributes the capacity to act.

The third volume identifies the “black holes of informational capitalism”: territories and groups may be not merely disadvantaged but structurally irrelevant to dominant networks (Castells, 1998). Digital exclusion is not the absence of a gadget but the absence of a position from which participation affects a decision. Connectivity without the capacity to program or switch may amount to subordinate inclusion.

The network nevertheless also creates counterpower. A movement can bypass a traditional center, connect local conflicts, and circulate its own frames of meaning. A counternetwork, however, confronts the same problem: it needs infrastructure, trust, attention, and durable code. An open protocol lowers the barrier without abolishing asymmetries of resources.

## The Limits of Castells's Theory

Critics have charged Castells with technological determinism and an exaggerated epochalism: networks and global flows existed long before the microprocessor, capital retains ownership, and the state retains the right to coerce (Stehr, 2000; Stalder, 1998). The objection is substantial. The concept of a network becomes empty if it denotes every connection; the concept of informationalism becomes circular if the growth of information is demonstrated by expanding the categories of informational labor.

The stronger version of the argument, however, does not require declaring a complete historical rupture. The novelty lies in the combination of programmability, speed, scale, and feedback. Railway and telegraph networks already organized flows; a digital network permits routing rules to be altered continuously and participants' behavior to be evaluated on the basis of data. Power becomes not less material but more heavily mediated by layers of standards and computation.

The phrase “power shifted to flows” should therefore be read as an analytical provocation. Power did not leave people and institutions. It moved toward the capacity to shape a flow: to encode, connect, accelerate, filter, store, decrypt, and exclude. In a network society, what governs is not the message itself but the architecture of its possible path.

# Conclusion. Not an Invention but an Agreement

The history before the Internet reveals not an approach toward a single machine but a sequence of redefinitions of information. For Bush, it was an expanding archive in need of an associative path. For Shannon, a probability distribution and a measure of choice. For Bell, codified knowledge as the axial resource of postindustrial structure. For Negroponte, bits liberated from one obligatory material carrier. For McLuhan and Rushkoff, an environment and a replicating cultural form. For Hughes, something whose disclosure the subject must be able to choose. For Castells, the content of flows and at the same time the basis of a new social morphology.

None of these definitions abolishes the others. A networked message exists simultaneously as a physical state, a coded sequence, an economic asset, a media form, a social action, and an object of law. The error of a monodisciplinary history is to select one level as the cause of all the rest. Bandwidth does not explain a business model; an open license does not guarantee political freedom; cryptographic strength does not create a just institution; viral circulation does not establish truth.

The nine sections support seven conclusions.

**First, the Internet had no single point of origin.** The year 1969 marks the operation of ARPANET; 1974, the formulation of an internetwork protocol; 1983, the transition to TCP/IP; 1989–1990, the creation of the Web; and 1993, the legal opening of its foundational software. Each date answers a different question.

**Second, the military context was a condition but not an exhaustive purpose.** The Cold War created ARPA and research into survivable distributed communication; an academic culture of resource sharing and open specifications directed the project toward a general-purpose infrastructure. Historical causation operates at multiple levels: the motive for funding is not identical to the engineer's motive and does not predetermine a user's application.

**Third, openness is a designed institution.** The Web spread through a combination of a minimal protocol, an accessible implementation, and the legal renunciation of royalties. Open architecture requires standards and organizations rather than an absence of rules. It is compatible with closed layers and must therefore be continually reproduced through politics.

**Fourth, digitalization relocates scarcity rather than abolishing it.** When a copy is inexpensive, the first trustworthy version, attention, discoverability, trust, unique data, and control of the channel become more valuable. The information economy is built on the mismatch between nonrival use and multiple forms of exclusion.

**Fifth, protocol is a form of power.** It determines permissible distinctions and distributes responsibility between center and edges. TCP/IP accommodates heterogeneous networks; the Web permits one-way linking; a cryptographic protocol limits an intermediary's knowledge. These decisions do not replace law, but they create facts with which law must contend.

**Sixth, media form the subject through rhythm and selection.** Electronic speed, the interface, and engagement metrics alter not only the circulation of completed content but the form of a statement capable of appearing. The user becomes author, audience, distributor, and data source at once.

**Seventh, power in a network society is concentrated in programming and switching.** The dominant actor is the one able to establish a standard, connect networks, manage visibility, authenticate identity, or exclude a node. Yet the same architecture permits counternetworks, open code, and distributed collaboration. A network is neither democratic nor authoritarian in itself; it raises the stakes of the struggle over its program.

In this light, the Internet may be defined as a historical agreement among incompatible systems. At the physical level, the agreement is constrained by noise and energy. At the technical level, it is expressed in protocol. At the economic level, it balances an expensive first copy against inexpensive reproduction. At the legal level, it distributes permissions and responsibility. At the cultural level, it establishes forms of attention. At the political level, it determines who may be a node, who becomes a flow, and who controls the switch.

“Before the Internet” does not end when the last component is connected. It persists within the contemporary network as a layer of unresolved questions. The memex recalls the durability of knowledge; Shannon, the limits of the channel; Brand, the conflict between price and freedom; Hughes, selective disclosure; and Castells, the power to connect and disconnect. The Internet's past matters not because it predicted the present correctly, but because it preserved alternatives that the present has grown accustomed to treating as impossible.

# Note on Sources

The original list supplied in the screenshot was checked against first editions, journal publications, and library metadata. Three bibliographic points were clarified.

1. Shannon's 1948 paper was titled *A Mathematical Theory of Communication* and appeared in two parts in volume 27 of the *Bell System Technical Journal*. The 1949 book edition with Warren Weaver was titled *The Mathematical Theory of Communication*.

2. “Information Wants to Be Free” is not the title of a stand-alone 1984 book by Stewart Brand. It was a remark made at the first Hackers Conference in November 1984 and published as part of the conference discussion in *Whole Earth Review* in May 1985. The complete pair of propositions matters: information tends toward freedom and, at the same time, toward expense.

3. Castells's *The Information Age* is a trilogy: volume I appeared in 1996, volume II in 1997, and volume III in 1998. This study uses the first English-language editions; the Alianza Editorial Spanish edition was consulted to compare structure and terminology.

Primary online documents were checked against official or institutional archives: the CERN Document Server and W3C for the history of the Web; DARPA, RAND/National Security Archive, and the RFC Editor for the history of networks; journal DOI records and author archives for technical papers; and the Cypherpunks mailing-list archive and EFF for the history of cryptographic policy. Web resources were checked on July 17, 2026.
